notes: Scope: 18 people (hacker-club founders, digital-rights advocates, security technologists, whistleblowers and journalists) who shaped the privacy debate, 11 events (CCC 1981 and the 1984 Btx hack; EFF 1990; DEF CON 1993; HOPE 1994; Barlow's 1996 declaration; WSJ 'What They Know' 2010; the CCC state-trojan analysis 2011; SecureDrop 2013; noyb 2017; the Clearview AI story 2020), 5 myths, and openly licensed portraits from Wikimedia Commons. Events already covered by other slices (Snowden/PRISM June 2013, Schrems I and II, Cambridge Analytica March 2018) are not duplicated here; the people cards link to them. Addition beyond the brief: Ashkan Soltani (What They Know technologist, co-creator of Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control, first CPPA executive director), for his direct bearing on machine-readable privacy signals. Verified cards were also drafted for Phil Zimmermann, Eric Hughes, David Chaum, Moxie Marlinspike and Doc Searls but removed before delivery because the parallel slices personas-code and personas-researchers already carry cards (and portraits) under the same ids. OVERLAP TO RECONCILE: 'john-gilmore' is in this file (as EFF co-founder, per this slice's brief: 1991 CFP talk, Gilmore v. Gonzales) and also in personas-code.json (as cypherpunk) — the editorial layer should merge the two cards. Method: each person researched one at a time; every quote copied from the fetched page and checked with tools/fetch-text.py --check (all quotes re-checked in a final pass). Where a site blocked the helper's browser user agent (schneier.com, upi.com etc.) the page was fetched with a descriptive research user agent into the same cache and then checked; where the helper's paragraph extractor skipped a div (one FSF page) the check was run against the page's full text and this is noted. Could not read directly (cited via secondary copies, noted per record): The New York Times Clearview article (403/JS wall; cited through EPIC's FOIA request and the ACLU), wsj.com 'What They Know' (paywall; read in a PDF compilation hosted by Cornell University), the ICO's 2 October 2020 letter to Parliament (bot challenge; read via TechCrunch), the Pulitzer site and parliament.uk (403), the CCC's scanned 1984 Btx documents (no text layer). Balance: controversies recorded where documented — Stallman's 2019 resignation and 2021 return to the FSF board; Greenwald's 2020 departure from The Intercept with the site's rebuttal; Cadwalladr's libel case (truth defence withdrawn, apology, claim dismissed 2022, appeal allowed in part 2023); Wylie as both architect and whistleblower; Snowden's Espionage Act charges and Russian citizenship; Poulsen's criminal record. Known conflicts: DEF CON's own archive dates DEF CON 1 to June 1993, but the organisers' June 1993 announcement and InfoWorld show 9–11 July 1993 (see myth). The CPPA dates the 'What They Know' Pulitzer finalist citation to 2012, Julia Angwin's biography to 2011 (unresolved). Portraits: Wikimedia was heavily rate-limited (HTTP 429) for most of the session; licences were read from the Commons API extmetadata and file-page wikitext, and only public-domain, CC0, CC BY and CC BY-SA files were used. Two portraits reference images already catalogued in research/media.json rather than duplicating them: edward-snowden-hong-kong-2013 and max-schrems-big-brother-awards-2015. A Laura Poitras 2014 portrait was rejected because its Commons description had been vandalised; the 2010 PopTech photo is used instead.

people.name: Herwart Holland-Moritz
people.roles: hacker · journalist · Chaos Computer Club co-founder

keyWork.title: The Btx hack (with Steffen Wernéry), exposing the Bundespost's Bildschirmtext service

people.contribution: Holland was one of five Hamburg media activists who, in a notice in the Berlin newspaper taz on 1 September 1981, invited 'Komputerfrieks' to the 12 September 1981 meeting that the Chaos Computer Club counts as its informal founding. In November 1984 he and Steffen Wernéry used a Hamburger Sparkasse login to run up DM 134,634.88 on a CCC page in the Bundespost's Btx system, then went public to show the service was insecure. He lectured for years on people caught between media technology and surveillance, and died on 29 July 2001.

people.influence: Friends and journalists credit Holland with fixing the pattern of CCC actions: expose a flaw, then go to the press to warn about weak security and insufficient data protection, which cast hackers in German public life as defenders of informational self-determination rather than computer criminals.

people.name: John Perry Barlow
people.roles: essayist · Grateful Dead lyricist · EFF co-founder

keyWork.title: A Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace

people.contribution: Barlow, a Wyoming rancher and Grateful Dead lyricist who met the 'electronic frontier' on the WELL, co-founded the Electronic Frontier Foundation with Mitch Kapor and John Gilmore in 1990 after the Secret Service raid on Steve Jackson Games. On 8 February 1996, the day the US Telecommunications Act (with its Communications Decency Act) became law, he wrote in Davos 'A Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace', rejecting government sovereignty over the online world. He died on 7 February 2018.
people.quote: Governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed. You have neither solicited nor received ours.

people.influence: By Barlow's own count the declaration was on at least 10,000 websites within a month and became the reference text of internet exceptionalism; twenty years on he conceded that the self-regulation it promised had, 'in most ways', not arrived, and EFF has defended him against the charge of naive techno-utopianism.
people.thread: The declaration rested legitimacy on consent and promised that users were 'forming our own Social Contract' — an early claim that the people online, not outside authorities, should write the terms.

people.name: John Gilmore

keyWork.title: 'Privacy, Technology, and the Open Society', talk at the First Conference on Computers, Freedom, and Privacy

people.contribution: An early Sun Microsystems employee and free-software entrepreneur, Gilmore co-founded the Electronic Frontier Foundation in 1990 and the Cypherpunks, and co-created EFF's DES Cracker. His March 1991 talk at the first Computers, Freedom and Privacy conference argued for privacy guaranteed by encryption rather than by law. On 4 July 2002 he refused to show ID for a Southwest Airlines flight and sued; in Gilmore v. Gonzales (2006) the Ninth Circuit reviewed the undisclosed identification policy, classed as 'sensitive security information', in camera and upheld it.

people.contribution: Kapor, former president of Lotus Development Corporation, co-founded the Electronic Frontier Foundation in 1990 and co-wrote its founding paper with Barlow. In Wired in 1993 he argued that the coming 'information highway' must be built as an open network with published interfaces, and that constitutional protections of privacy should extend to it. He is credited with the maxim 'Architecture is politics', which he dated to 1991.

people.name: Richard M. Stallman
people.roles: programmer · founder of GNU and the Free Software Foundation
people.place: MIT Artificial Intelligence Lab, Cambridge, Massachusetts

keyWork.title: The GNU Project announcement ('Free Unix!') and the Free Software Definition

people.contribution: On 27 September 1983 Stallman, then at MIT's Artificial Intelligence Lab, announced GNU, a Unix-compatible system he would give away free, and went on to found the Free Software Foundation. His free-software definition makes user control of software a moral question: users should be free to run, copy, distribute, study, change and improve programs. After the Snowden disclosures he argued in Wired (October 2013) that general surveillance had reached a level incompatible with human rights. He resigned as FSF president on 16 September 2019 amid controversy and returned to its board in 2021, a decision the board acknowledged some found troubling.

people.name: Cory Doctorow

keyWork.title: Privacy Without Monopoly: Data Protection and Interoperability (EFF white paper, with Bennett Cyphers)

people.contribution: Toronto-born Doctorow, a former European director of the Electronic Frontier Foundation and co-founder of the UK's Open Rights Group, writes fiction and non-fiction about surveillance, including the young-adult novel Little Brother and the book How to Destroy Surveillance Capitalism. With EFF technologist Bennett Cyphers he co-wrote the February 2021 white paper Privacy Without Monopoly, which argues that big platforms' privacy failures and their market power are linked. It proposed mandates for data portability, back-end interoperability and 'delegability' — letting users' own software act on platforms for them.
people.quote: Delegability would set in stone the right to outsource privacy decisions.

people.influence: Doctorow's books and EFF work popularised the argument that surveillance is an effect of platform monopoly and that the remedy includes interoperability — tools that let users 'wrest control of their data from big platforms', in EFF's words.
people.thread: The white paper's 'delegated agents' — software a user authorises to act on a platform for them — anticipate agents that carry a person's own privacy terms: 'These “delegated agents” will be able to tip the balance of power between users and platforms so that users come out on top.'

people.name: Bruce Schneier

people.contribution: A security technologist who has published the Crypto-Gram newsletter since 1998 and his blog since 2004, Schneier argued after the Snowden disclosures that government mass surveillance was built on corporate tracking — 'the public/private surveillance partnership'. His March 2015 book Data and Goliath, a New York Times best seller, set out how states and companies collect data and proposed reforms to both. He lectures at the Harvard Kennedy School, sits on EFF's board and is Chief of Security Architecture at Inrupt, which commercialises Tim Berners-Lee's Solid personal-data pods.

people.name: Aaron Swartz

keyWork.title: DeadDrop, the anonymous document-submission system later renamed SecureDrop (with Kevin Poulsen)

people.contribution: Swartz, one of the three coders who sold Reddit to Condé Nast in 2006 and an activist for open information, built tools for anonymous publishing: in October 2008 he released a tor2web proxy so that ordinary browsers could reach sites hidden on Tor. From 2011 he coded, with Wired editor Kevin Poulsen, an open-source 'anonymous in-box' for journalists' sources, which they called DeadDrop; the code was stable by December 2012. Swartz, then under federal indictment for bulk-downloading about four million JSTOR articles at MIT, took his own life on 11 January 2013; the system launched at The New Yorker as Strongbox on 14 May 2013.

people.influence: The submission system he wrote became SecureDrop, which the Freedom of the Press Foundation took over in October 2013 to install in newsrooms, making source anonymity a piece of standard newsroom infrastructure.

people.name: Kevin Poulsen

keyWork.title: DeadDrop / Strongbox, the anonymous source-submission system built with Aaron Swartz

people.contribution: In the late 1980s and early 1990s Poulsen was a notorious hacker: federal prosecutors charged him in 1993 with seizing Pacific Bell phone lines to win Los Angeles radio contests and with setting up his own wiretaps, and he pleaded guilty, including to breaking into a computer for the names of FBI undercover businesses. He became a journalist and Wired's investigations editor, and in 2011 asked Aaron Swartz to build an open-source anonymous in-box for sources. After Swartz's death he launched it as Strongbox at The New Yorker in May 2013 and handed it to the Freedom of the Press Foundation, which renamed it SecureDrop, in October 2013.

people.name: Edward Snowden

people.contribution: Snowden, a 29-year-old Booz Allen Hamilton employee working at the NSA and a former CIA technical assistant, gave journalists top-secret documents on US and allied mass surveillance, then flew to Hong Kong on 20 May 2013 and identified himself in the Guardian on 9 June 2013. The disclosures began with the bulk collection of Americans' phone records. A criminal complaint dated 14 June 2013 charged him with theft of government property and two Espionage Act offences; he has lived in Russia since 2013 and was granted Russian citizenship by decree in September 2022.

events.title: Kapor and Barlow announce the Electronic Frontier Foundation
events.summary: After a 1 March 1990 Secret Service raid on Steve Jackson Games in Austin, Texas, in which the company's bulletin-board e-mail was accessed and deleted, Mitch Kapor, John Perry Barlow and John Gilmore formed an organisation for civil liberties raised by new technologies. Kapor and Barlow announced the Electronic Frontier Foundation in Washington on 10 July 1990, with a founding paper asking whether 'the history of one's personal business affairs' could properly belong to someone else. EFF's first case, for Steve Jackson Games, led a court to hold that e-mail deserves at least as much protection as telephone calls.
events.significance: Created the first advocacy organisation built to argue for privacy and speech rights inside networks, and framed personal data as something that might belong to the person.

sources.title: Mitchell Kapor and John Perry Barlow, 'Across the Electronic Frontier'
sources.quote: Can the history of one's personal business affairs properly belong to someone else?
sources.note: Dateline on the page: 'Electronic Frontier Foundation Washington, D.C. July 10, 1990'. Also FOUND: 'We are founding the Electronic Frontier Foundation to deal with these and related challenges.'

sources.title: Lucy Bernholz, 'The Invention of Digital Civil Society' (Summer 2019)
sources.quote: Then, on July 10, 1990, at the National Press Club in Washington, D.C., software developer Mitch Kapor and Grateful Dead lyricist John Perry Barlow announced the creation of the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) to protect people’s rights on the Internet, or “electronic frontier.”
sources.note: The same article dates the Steve Jackson Games raid to 1 March 1990. It also records later criticism: 'But contemporary critics of EFF now fault this focus, pointing to corporate surveillance as an equal threat.'

sources.title: About EFF: History
sources.quote: The Electronic Frontier Foundation was founded in July of 1990 in response to a basic threat to speech and privacy.
sources.note: Also FOUND: 'For the first time, a court held that electronic mail deserves at least as much protection as telephone calls.' The page names Kapor, Barlow and Gilmore as founders, 'with assistance from Steve Wozniak'. Undated organisational page; date is the access year. Also on this page: stored e-mail on the Steve Jackson Games bulletin board 'had been individually accessed and deleted'.

events.locationNote: Announcement site (National Press Club, 529 14th St NW). EFF's first office was at 155 Second Street, Cambridge, Massachusetts, per Barlow's November 1990 'A Not Terribly Brief History of the Electronic Frontier Foundation' (eff.org).

events.title: Barlow's 'Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace'
events.place: Davos, Switzerland (World Economic Forum annual meeting)
events.summary: On 8 February 1996, the day President Clinton signed the Telecommunications Act of 1996 with its Communications Decency Act, John Perry Barlow wrote a manifesto at the close of the World Economic Forum in Davos telling 'Governments of the Industrial World' they had no sovereignty online. He e-mailed it to about 600 friends the next day; by his count it was on at least 10,000 websites within a month. Twenty years later Barlow stood by it while conceding that online self-regulation had in most ways not developed.
events.significance: The founding text of the claim that people online could set their own rules, the libertarian starting point that later privacy advocates both built on and argued against.

sources.title: John Perry Barlow, 'A Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace'
sources.quote: In the United States, you have today created a law, the Telecommunications Reform Act, which repudiates your own Constitution and insults the dreams of Jefferson, Washington, Mill, Madison, DeToqueville, and Brandeis.
sources.note: Signed 'Davos, Switzerland February 8, 1996'.

sources.title: Public Law 104-104, Telecommunications Act of 1996
sources.quote: Approved February 8, 1996.
sources.note: Title V of the Act is the Communications Decency Act of 1996.

sources.title: John Perry Barlow, 'Reflections, 20 years Later, on A Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace'
sources.quote: At the end of a month, it appeared, using the primitive tools of the day, to be on at least 10,000 Internet sites.
sources.note: The same text says he wrote it at 'a staff party for the closing of the World Economic Forum' and sent it 'the next day to the 600 or so friends I had with e-mail addresses'.

events.locationNote: Davos Congress Centre area; Barlow wrote the text at a WEF closing party whose exact venue is not recorded.

events.title: The first DEF CON puts hackers, lawyers and a prosecutor in one room
events.place: Sands Hotel & Casino, Las Vegas, Nevada
events.summary: Jeff Moss ('The Dark Tangent'), organising from Seattle, turned a farewell party for a bulletin-board friend into a convention, inviting 'hackers/phreaks, techno-rats, programmers, writers, activists, lawyers, philosophers, politicians, security officials' to the Sands Hotel, Las Vegas, on Friday to Sunday 9–11 July 1993, at $30 at the door. InfoWorld's Robert X. Cringely reported that the Operation Sun Devil prosecutor spoke and told the young crowd 'I'm not here to bust you'. Billed as the '1st annual Def Con', it grew into a gathering that The Record put at some 30,000 hackers in 2025.
events.significance: Created a standing meeting ground where hackers, security staff, lawyers and law enforcement argue in public over surveillance, security and privacy.

sources.title: DEF CON I Convention — Finalized Announcement (12 June 1993)
sources.quote: WHEN: July 9th, 10th and 11th (Fri, Sat, Sun) 1993
sources.note: Plain-text announcement headed 'Finalized Announcement: 6/12/1993'. Also FOUND: 'DEF CON I will be over the weekend in the middle of down town Las Vegas at the Sands Hotel.' and the invitation list quoted in the summary. 9 July 1993 was a Friday. DEF CON's own archive page (https://defcon.org/html/links/dc-archives/dc-1-archive.html) says 'Was June 9-11, 1993' — see myth record.

sources.title: Robert X. Cringely, 'DoubleSpace may not scan your hardware, but DEF CON denizens do', InfoWorld, 19 July 1993, p. 98
sources.quote: DEF CON I, last week in Las Vegas, was both the strangest and the best computer event I have attended in years.
sources.note: Also FOUND: 'And several of the hackers present (median age 17) were shaken to find their Operation Sun Devil prosecutor sitting in the back of the room (she was one of the speakers).' Transcript hosted by DEF CON; the original is in InfoWorld's 19 July 1993 issue.

sources.title: Jeff Moss on DEF CON and its shadow power
sources.quote: In the summer of 1993, someone on Moss’s Platinum Net BBS network was moving out of town and suggested a farewell party.
sources.note: Same article: Moss 'called himself “The Dark Tangent”', and DEF CON is now 'where researchers expose vulnerabilities in satellites and voting machines'.

events.locationNote: The Sands Hotel & Casino, since demolished; coordinates of its former site on the Las Vegas Strip.

events.title: Hackers On Planet Earth: 2600's first HOPE conference
events.place: Hotel Pennsylvania, Manhattan, New York City
events.summary: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly marked its tenth anniversary with Hackers On Planet Earth, held at the Hotel Pennsylvania in Manhattan on 13–14 August 1994 and attended by well over 1,000 people. Modelled on the Dutch hacker gatherings of the 1980s and 1990s, it was the first US hacker conference on that scale, with talks 'ranging from privacy issues to technology to politics' and a panel on cryptography and privacy. HOPE became a recurring New York conference, annual from 2025.
events.significance: Gave the hacker scene around 2600 a large public forum in New York where surveillance, cryptography and privacy were argued before a mass audience.

sources.title: Hackers On Planet Earth
sources.quote: Hackers On Planet Earth, a conference in New York City, marking 2600 Magazine's 10 year anniversary, took place on August 13th-14th of 1994.
sources.note: Also FOUND: 'Well over 1000 people were in attendance at this gala event.' and 'Speakers from around the world made presentations ranging from privacy issues to technology to politics to methodologies.'

sources.title: About HOPE
sources.quote: The first Hackers On Planet Earth (HOPE) conference took place at the Hotel Pennsylvania in Manhattan, New York City over two days.
sources.note: Same page: 'It was the first time that a hacker conference of this size had been attempted in the United States and it was inspired by the Dutch hacker gatherings of the 80s and 90s.' and 'In 2025, for the first time ever, HOPE became an annual event.' The 2600 store lists a 1994 recording titled 'Cryptography and Privacy' (https://store.2600.com/collections/hackers-on-planet-earth).

events.locationNote: Hotel Pennsylvania, Seventh Avenue, Manhattan — HOPE's usual venue until The Circle of HOPE, the last HOPE held there (per hope.net/about).

events.title: Aaron Swartz's DeadDrop becomes SecureDrop
events.place: Freedom of the Press Foundation, San Francisco, California
events.summary: Four months after the first Snowden stories, the Freedom of the Press Foundation announced on 15 October 2013 that it had taken over DeadDrop, the whistleblower-submission system coded by Aaron Swartz with Kevin Poulsen, renamed it SecureDrop and would install it in newsrooms. Each source receives a codename so they can keep talking to a newsroom without revealing their identity or using e-mail. The code had been audited by University of Washington researchers; The New Yorker, the first user since May 2013 under the name Strongbox, kept its installation.
events.significance: Made source anonymity a standard, shareable piece of newsroom infrastructure — privacy enforced by system design rather than by a publisher's promise.

sources.title: Freedom of the Press Foundation Launches SecureDrop, an Open-Source Submission Platform for Whistleblowers
sources.quote: Each source who uses the platform is assigned a unique codename that lets the source establish a relationship with the news organization without having to reveal her real identity or resort to e-mail.
sources.note: Dateline FOUND: 'October 15, 2013 San Francisco, CA : Freedom of the Press Foundation has taken charge of the DeadDrop project'. Also FOUND: the University of Washington audit sentence, and that 'The New Yorker, the first news organization to use the SecureDrop code, through its StrongBox project , will continue to operate its system.'

sources.quote: The New Yorker ’ s version is called Strongbox; it went online this morning .
sources.note: The spacing reproduces the page text as extracted.

events.locationNote: Dateline of the announcement: San Francisco, California (city centroid).

events.title: Max Schrems founds noyb to enforce the GDPR against companies
events.summary: noyb ('none of your business'), the European Center for Digital Rights, was founded in Vienna on 12 June 2017 by Max Schrems, who had brought down the EU–US Safe Harbour framework. Crowdfunded towards a €500,000 target, it set out to focus on commercial privacy violations and to use GDPR Article 80 to bring collective complaints; it became operational on 1 February 2018 and filed its first cases on 25 May 2018, the GDPR's first day, against 'forced consent' at Google, Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram.
events.significance: Created a standing enforcer that turns individuals' GDPR rights into collective action against platforms — the institutional counterpart to people asserting their own terms.

sources.institution: noyb – European Center for Digital Rights
sources.title: Information in accordance with Directive (EU) 2020/1828 on Collective Redress
sources.quote: noyb was founded on 12.06.2017 and became operational on 01.02.2018. We filed our first cases on 25.05.2018
sources.note: noyb's about page (https://noyb.eu/en/about-us), FOUND: 'noyb is a donation-funded NGO based in Vienna, Austria working to enforce data protection laws, in particular the GDPR and the ePrivacy Directive.'

sources.quote: NOYB, however, will focus on commercial privacy violations.
sources.note: Also FOUND: 'To date, NOYB has raised 55,316 euros; its goal is 500,000.' and the Article 80 sentence. Page metadata shows 2023 (site migration); the text refers to the launch as current, placing it in late 2017 — exact date not confirmed.

sources.quote: On the first day of GDPR noyb.eu has therefore filed four complaints against Google (Android), Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram over “forced consent”.

events.title: The Wall Street Journal's 'What They Know' counts the trackers
events.place: The Wall Street Journal newsroom, Midtown Manhattan, New York City
events.summary: On 30 July 2010 The Wall Street Journal opened 'What They Know', an investigation led by Julia Angwin with technical consultant Ashkan Soltani, with 'The Web's New Gold Mine: Your Secrets'. Testing the 50 most popular US websites, the Journal found they installed an average of 64 pieces of tracking technology — cookies, Flash cookies and beacons — on a visitor's computer, usually with no warning. Later instalments covered mobile apps, device fingerprinting and how Microsoft's advertising side blocked stronger privacy features planned for Internet Explorer 8.
events.significance: Measured the third-party tracking economy for a mass audience and fed Congressional and FTC efforts to rein in the tracking industry.

sources.institution: The Wall Street Journal (compilation hosted by Cornell University, CS 5436 course page)
sources.title: What They Know: The Business of Tracking You on the Internet — A Wall Street Journal Investigation
sources.quote: The study found that the nation's 50 top websites on average installed 64 pieces of tracking technology onto the computers of ... visitors, usually with no warning.
sources.note: The ellipsis bridges a page-footer break in the PDF. The article is marked 'Published July 30, 2010.' The compilation's table of contents lists later instalments including 'Microsoft Quashed Effort To Boost Online Privacy', 'Race Is On To ‘Fingerprint’ Phones, PCs' and 'Your Apps Are Watching You'. Original: wsj.com (paywalled).

sources.title: The Wall Street Journal Asks: What Do Online Advertisers Know About You?
sources.quote: It's already affecting the conversation in Washington DC, where important efforts by both Congress and the FTC are underway to rein in this dangerous and unregulated industry.

events.locationNote: Approximate coordinates of the Journal's Midtown Manhattan headquarters; the series was also a web project with interactive data.

events.title: Kashmir Hill exposes Clearview AI's scraped face database
events.place: The New York Times newsroom, Manhattan, New York City
events.summary: The New York Times article 'The Secretive Company That Might End Privacy as We Know It' by Kashmir Hill, dated 18 January 2020 in its web address, revealed that the start-up Clearview AI had scraped more than three billion images from Facebook, YouTube, Venmo, Twitter and other sites and that more than 600 law-enforcement agencies had begun using its face-search app within a year. After the story, New Jersey's attorney general barred state police from using it, Vermont's attorney general sued and members of Congress demanded answers; Australia's privacy regulator opened inquiries on 21 January 2020 and in October 2021 ordered the company to stop collecting and to destroy Australians' images.
events.significance: Showed that anything a person posts can be harvested into a biometric identification system without consent — and that after-the-fact 'opt-out' forms are no substitute for terms set before collection.

sources.title: EPIC FOIA request to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement on Clearview AI (6 March 2020)
sources.quote: Clearview has scraped more than 3 billion images from websites and social media platforms such as Facebook, YouTube, Venmo, and Twitter.
sources.note: Also FOUND: 'Within the past year, more than 600 law enforcement agencies have started using the Clearview AI app.' Both sentences are footnoted to the Times article, cited as 'Kashmir Hill, The Secretive Company That Might End Privacy as We Know It, N.Y. Times (Feb. 10, 2020), https://www.nytimes.com/2020/01/18/technology/clearview-privacy-facial-recognition.html' (the Feb. 10 date is a later update; the URL carries the 18 January 2020 original). The Times page itself blocks scripted access (403/JS wall) and was not read.

sources.title: ACLU Sues Clearview AI (press release)
sources.quote: Following the NYT story, the New Jersey attorney general prohibited state law enforcement from using Clearview’s system, the Vermont attorney general sued, and members of Congress demanded answers.
sources.note: Also FOUND: 'Clearview gained national attention after the New York Times revealed the company was secretly capturing untold numbers of biometric identifiers for purposes of surveillance and tracking, without notice to the individuals affected.' The ACLU is a party to litigation against Clearview.

sources.institution: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner
sources.title: Commissioner initiated investigation into Clearview AI, Inc. (Privacy) [2021] AICmr 54 (14 October 2021)
sources.quote: On 21 January 2020, the OAIC sent preliminary inquiries to the respondent
sources.note: The determination orders that Clearview 'must cease to collect Scraped Images, Probe Images, Scraped Image Vectors, Probe Image Vectors and Opt-out Vectors' from individuals in Australia and destroy those held; it records that 'From 29 January 2020, it began to offer Australian residents an online form to ‘opt-out’' which later 'became no longer accessible'.

events.locationNote: Approximate coordinates of the Times building in Midtown Manhattan. The ACLU describes Clearview as 'a little-known start-up based in New York' (https://www.aclu.org/news/privacy-technology/were-taking-clearview-ai-to-court-to-end-its-privacy-destroying-face-surveillance-activities).

myths.claim: The first DEF CON was held on 9–11 June 1993.
myths.correction: The June date appears on DEF CON's own archive page and is widely repeated, but the organisers' finalized announcement, dated 12 June 1993, gives 'July 9th, 10th and 11th (Fri, Sat, Sun) 1993' — 9 July 1993 was a Friday — and InfoWorld's issue of 19 July 1993 described DEF CON I as 'last week in Las Vegas'. The first DEF CON took place on 9–11 July 1993.

sources.title: DEF CON I Convention — Finalized Announcement (12 June 1993)
sources.quote: WHEN: July 9th, 10th and 11th (Fri, Sat, Sun) 1993

sources.title: Robert X. Cringely, 'DoubleSpace may not scan your hardware, but DEF CON denizens do', InfoWorld, 19 July 1993, p. 98
sources.quote: DEF CON I, last week in Las Vegas, was both the strangest and the best computer event I have attended in years.

sources.title: DEF CON 1 Archive
sources.quote: Was June 9-11, 1993 at the Sands Hotel & Casino (Since Blown-up)
sources.note: The source of the popular June date; cited to document the error, not as support for it.

myths.claim: Cambridge Analytica used the harvested Facebook profiles to swing the 2016 Brexit referendum with psychological 'mind-control' targeting.
myths.correction: The UK Information Commissioner, closing its investigation in October 2020, concluded that the data Aleksandr Kogan's company supplied 'could not have been used in the Brexit Referendum' because it related to US registered voters, and that the firm's claims about the depth of its profiling 'may have been an exaggeration'. The harvesting itself — tens of millions of profiles, including friends who never used the app — was real, and a Canadian firm linked to Cambridge Analytica's parent, AIQ, did target ads for several Leave campaigns.

sources.institution: TechCrunch (reporting the UK Information Commissioner's letter to Parliament of 2 October 2020)
sources.title: Cambridge Analytica sought to use Facebook data to predict partisanship for voter targeting, UK investigation confirms
sources.quote: “Our view on review of the evidence is that the data from GSR could not have been used in the Brexit Referendum as the data shared with SCL/Cambridge Analytica by Dr Kogan related to US registered voters,” it writes.
sources.note: Also FOUND: '“Based on what we found it appears that this may have been an exaggeration,” it writes.' and 'The ICO’s letter also discusses the Canada-based data company AIQ, which was linked to CA/SCL, and did play a key role in the UK’s Brexit referendum — as it was used by several ‘Leave’ campaigns to target ads at UK voters via Facebook.' The ICO letter itself (committees.parliament.uk/publications/2847/documents/27859/default/) was behind a bot challenge and could not be read directly.

sources.title: Carole Cadwalladr and Emma Graham-Harrison, 'Revealed: 50 million Facebook profiles harvested for Cambridge Analytica in major data breach'
sources.quote: However, the app also collected the information of the test-takers’ Facebook friends, leading to the accumulation of a data pool tens of millions-strong.

myths.claim: In 1984 Chaos Computer Club hackers robbed a Hamburg savings bank of about DM 135,000.
myths.correction: The 'bank robbery' was a demonstration. Using the Hamburger Sparkasse's Btx login, a program called a CCC page priced at DM 9.97 13,504 times overnight, running up a virtual DM 134,634.88 that 'theoretically went to the CCC'. The club had warned the Bundespost and data-protection officials in October 1984 and went public at once, calling for a ban on financial transactions on Btx.

sources.title: 40 years ago: the Btx hack celebrates a happy birthday
sources.quote: Not only the public, but also the Btx operators were surprised by the action, with which the CCC was able to collect a virtual DM 134,634.88.
sources.note: Also FOUND: 'For every call to this page, there were 9.97 marks, which theoretically went to the CCC.'

sources.title: BTX Hack 30th Year Anniversary
sources.quote: Steffen Wernéry and Wau Holland showed how unsecure the BTX system from the Deutsche Bundespost was for its users with their so-called "bank theft" of 135.000 DM; this unconventional demonstration made history.

myths.claim: Wau Holland founded the Chaos Computer Club.
myths.correction: Holland was a co-founder and the club's best-known voice, but the taz notice of 1 September 1981 that called the founding meeting was signed by five Hamburg men — Klaus Schleisiek ('Tom Twiddlebit'), Wau Holland, Wolf Gevert and two unnamed others later identified as Wulf Müller and Jochen Büttner — and about 20 people attended the 12 September 1981 meeting in Berlin.

sources.institution: Universität Hamburg (M.A. thesis), hosted by stummkonzert.de
sources.title: Matthias Röhr, 'Ursprünge und Entwicklung des Chaos Computer Clubs in den 1980er Jahren' (version 1.11, 15 May 2014)
sources.quote: Unter dem Pseudonym Tom Twiddlebit verbarg sich Klaus Schleisiek, Wau stand für Herwart Holland-Moritz, genannt Wau Holland, mit Wolf war Wolf Gevert gemeint.
sources.note: Translation: 'Behind the pseudonym Tom Twiddlebit was Klaus Schleisiek; Wau stood for Herwart Holland-Moritz, known as Wau Holland; Wolf meant Wolf Gevert.' The thesis continues: 'Die zwei Ungenannten waren Wulf Müller und Jochen Büttner' and 'Zu dem Treffen sollen etwa 20 Personen gekommen sein' (both FOUND).

myths.claim: John Perry Barlow delivered 'A Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace' as a speech to world leaders at the Davos World Economic Forum.
myths.correction: Barlow wrote the text at Davos but not as a speech: by his own account he wrote it during a party at the close of the 1996 World Economic Forum, as a contribution to the book 24 Hours in Cyberspace (whose editors found it too controversial to use), and e-mailed it the next day to about 600 friends, from where it spread online.

sources.title: John Perry Barlow, 'Reflections, 20 years Later, on A Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace'
sources.quote: Eventually, I just hit "send" and dispatched the piece to the editors of 24 Hours in Cyberspace (who found it too controversial to include in their coffee table book).
sources.note: Also FOUND: 'Twenty years ago tonight, I was at a staff party for the closing of the World Economic Forum' and 'I sent it out the next day to the 600 or so friends I had with e-mail addresses'.

sources.title: Cory Doctorow, 'Celebrating the 20th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence of Cyberspace'
sources.quote: sat down in Davos, Switzerland, where he'd been addressing world leaders on the subject of the Internet and human rights, and wrote one of net-culture's formative documents
sources.note: Shows the accurate framing — he wrote it after taking part in the forum — from which the 'speech to world leaders' version drifts. Byline from the page's author meta tag (Cory Doctorow).
